The Challenge

The Next Israeli Frontier: Driving Resilience in East Africa

East Africa faces urgent climate and economic shifts that create a unique opportunity for Israeli tech entrepreneurs to solve and scale.

East Africa is one of the world's fastest-growing regions, expanding at 5–6% GDP growth per year. It is a market of extraordinary momentum, and one still shaped by challenges deep enough to build ventures around.

Those resilience challenges are real, and they are compounding. Since the 1970s, severe droughts across the region have tripled and extreme floods have risen more than tenfold, locking agriculture — which employs over 60% of East Africa's workforce — into a cycle of deepening climate volatility. Up to 40–50% of fruits and vegetables spoil before they reach consumers, driven by gaps in storage, cold chains, and rural infrastructure.

The infrastructure gaps run deeper still. Across Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania alone, more than 82 million people live without reliable electricity and over 60 million without access to clean drinking water — most of them smallholder farmers already on the front line of every climate shock. Large-scale infrastructure building is slow and costly, leaving the communities that need it most without a foundation to grow on.

Capital is scarce where it counts too: close to 70% of MSMEs across the three countries cannot access the formal financing they need — a shortfall of roughly $35 billion across Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. Without capital to invest, absorb shocks, or scale, even strong businesses stay fragile.

Read another way, every one of these numbers is a market opportunity. And East Africa's response is already underway. Kenya and its neighbors have become one of the continent's true innovation frontiers. Nairobi ranks as Africa's third-largest startup ecosystem, behind only Lagos and Cairo, drawing nearly $1 billion in venture funding in 2025, with clean energy, e-mobility, agri-tech, and water-tech leading the flow. The region adopts technology fast, its population is young and entrepreneurial, and its doors are open to Israeli innovation.

For an Israeli entrepreneur, this is rare terrain. The problems are urgent and worth solving. The environment is tech-friendly and fast-moving. And the partnerships run on trust and shared interest — an edge few others can claim.

East Africa is not just a growing market. It is a place where the right venture, built alongside local partners and aimed at real needs, can create lasting resilience for the people it serves, and a durable business for the people who build it.

This is your chance to build something that lasts, where it matters most.

The 2026 Pears Challenge is where you build it.

The challenges we are looking at

The Pears Challenge focus areas

We are seeking startups and venture ideas that tackle specific, real-world challenges in one of these focus areas:

Resilient food systems & climate adaptation

Goal: Empowering farming communities, strengthening domestic food production and export capabilities, and improving supply chains from production to markets, while strengthening systems to withstand climate change shocks and supporting environmental and regenerative agriculture practices.

Agri-TechFood-TechClimate-TechAquacul-Tech

Resilient infrastructure & supply chains

Goal: Ensuring quality and uninterrupted access to clean water, safely managed sanitation, reliable energy, transportation, and essential services for both rapidly growing urban centers and rural communities.

WaterTechEnergyTechLogiTechInfraTech & Smart Cities

Resilient finance & business continuity

Goal: Improving economic stability and household incomes of small and medium farmers, market traders, and local MSMEs against climate and economic shocks.

Who we’re looking for

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the program for?

The program is for early-stage ventures and startup ideas looking to validate their concept in East Africa. Ideal applicants have an existing venture idea ranging from theoretical concept to early-product that targets emerging markets and has a strong impact mission. We look for open-minded, impact-oriented, and experienced professionals/teams who are ready to validate their idea and take it to the next level.

We seek out equal gender representation and diversity in our cohorts and encourage applications from people of all ages, ethnicities, and religious backgrounds.

When does the program run?

The 2026 cohort runs from the selection phase in September–October 2026 through bootcamp, remote validation, and an on-the-ground field validation trip in early 2027, followed by a navigation and scale phase.

Are you ready to immerse?

We look for founders who are open-minded and eager to dive deep into the East African context — ready to spend time on the ground, listen to local partners and users, and adapt their idea for emerging markets.

Is there a program fee associated with Pears Challenge?

No. There is no fee to participate in the Pears Challenge. The program is fully funded, and selected ventures also access a mini-grant to help them scale.

Can I still work while participating in Pears Challenge: Validate?

Yes. The program is designed to run alongside your existing commitments, with a hybrid format and roughly part-time weekly involvement — though the in-person bootcamp and field validation trip require dedicated time.

Does the Pears Challenge take any equity in my venture?

No. The Pears Challenge is equity-free. We take no ownership in participating ventures — all mentorship, funding, and support is non-dilutive.

If I already have a venture idea or a working product, is the program right for me?

Yes. We welcome ventures from early concept through to an early product with initial traction. Whether you are validating a new idea or refining an existing product for East African markets, the program meets you where you are.
